problems.title: Which index drives x?
problems.statement: A 4096 × 4096 row-major float matrix, 32 × 8 blocks, accessed as a[y * 4096 + x].

parts.prompt: Sectors per warp load with x from threadIdx.x?
With x and y swapped (x from threadIdx.y, y from threadIdx.x)?

hints: Swapped: consecutive lanes differ in y.
problems.solution: (a) 32 consecutive floats: 4 sectors. (b) Consecutive lanes are a row apart (16 KB): every lane gets its own sector, 32.

problems.title: Particles, AoS and SoA
problems.statement: Particles with fields x, y, vx, vy (floats). A warp reads x for 32 consecutive particles.
problems.solution: AoS: lanes 16 bytes apart, 512 bytes spanned, 16 sectors, 25%. SoA: 4 sectors, 100%.

problems.title: A three-field struct
problems.statement: AoS of 12-byte structs {x, y, z}. A warp reads all three fields of 32 consecutive structs, one field per instruction.

parts.prompt: Sector requests for all three instructions?

hints: 32 structs span 384 bytes = 12 sectors, whichever field you read.
problems.solution: Each instruction touches all 12 sectors of the 384-byte span: 36 requests for 12 sectors of data. SoA: 3 × 4 = 12. If L1 catches the repeats, DRAM traffic is the same, but the 3× request count still costs L1 bandwidth and issue slots.

problems.title: Pitch
problems.statement: A float image is 1001 pixels wide. Rows are stored back to back from a 128-byte-aligned base. Warps read 32 consecutive pixels starting at x = 0, 32, 64, … of a row.

parts.prompt: Average sectors per warp load, over 8 consecutive rows?
Smallest row pitch (in floats, ≥ 1001) that makes every row start 32-byte aligned?
Smallest pitch that makes every row start 128-byte aligned?

hints: Row y starts at byte 4004y; 4004y mod 32 = 4y mod 32.
Pitch × 4 must be a multiple of 32 (or 128).
problems.solution: (a) Row starts are 32-byte aligned only every 8th row; the other 7 cost 5 sectors per warp: $(4 + 35)/8 = 4.875$. (b) 1008 floats = 4032 bytes = 126 sectors. (c) 1024 floats = 4096 bytes. cudaMallocPitch picks such a pitch for you and returns it.

problems.title: Thread per row, or thread per column?
problems.statement: Each thread sums one line of an N × N row-major matrix (N = 4096), looping over the other index.

parts.prompt: Thread ℓ sums row ℓ: sectors per warp load?
Thread ℓ sums column ℓ: sectors per warp load?

hints: At each loop step, which addresses do the 32 lanes read?
problems.solution: (a) Lanes read the same column position of 32 different rows: 16 KB apart, 32 sectors. (b) Lanes read 32 consecutive elements of the same row: 4 sectors. The "natural" row sum is the uncoalesced one; it needs a warp (or block) per row instead (Lab 5 does exactly this for GEMV).

problems.title: RGB bytes
problems.statement: An interleaved RGB8 image; one thread per pixel reads its R byte (lane ℓ reads byte 3ℓ).

parts.prompt: If 24 lanes instead each read one 4-byte word of the warp's 96 bytes: sectors?

problems.solution: (a) 3 sectors, (b) 32 useful bytes of 96: 33%; reading G and B costs 2 more instructions on the same sectors. (c) Cooperative word loads fetch the same 3 sectors in one instruction at 100%, then pixels are unpacked from shared memory or registers. That's milestone A2's trick.

problems.title: Sorting gathers
problems.statement: A warp gathers a[idx[i]]. Unsorted, idx is random over a huge array. After sorting idx, each warp's 32 indices fall uniformly at random within a window of 64 consecutive floats (8 sectors).
hints: Expected distinct sectors among 32 draws from 8.
problems.solution: (a) 32. (b) $8(1 - (7/8)^{32}) = 7.89$. (c) 4.1×. Sorting indices (or binning work by address) turns random gathers into nearly coalesced ones.

problems.title: The naive transpose
problems.statement: Transpose a 4096 × 4096 float matrix: thread (x, y) reads a[y][x] and writes b[x][y], 32 × 8 blocks.

parts.prompt: Overall efficiency (useful bytes / bytes moved), in %?

hints: Writes: consecutive lanes write consecutive rows of b.
problems.solution: (a) 4, (b) 32, (c) 256 useful bytes over 36 sectors (1,152 bytes): 22.2%. One side of a transpose is always strided; shared memory fixes it (2.5).

problems.title: Spot the coalesced access
problems.statement: 1-D index i from the global thread index unless stated; 2-D blocks are 32 × 8.

parts.prompt: Which accesses are fully coalesced (4 sectors per warp for floats)?
options: a[y*w + x], x from threadIdx.x, w a multiple of 32

problems.solution: a[2*i] is stride 2 (8 sectors). a[x*h + y] puts consecutive lanes h floats apart. The others are contiguous per warp.

problems.title: Narrow blocks
problems.statement: Read a[y*4096 + x] with x from threadIdx.x and different block widths. Count sectors per warp.
hints: 8 floats are exactly one sector; 4 floats are half a sector.
problems.solution: (a) One row of 32: 4 sectors. (b) Four rows of 8 floats, each exactly one aligned sector: still 4. (c) Eight rows of 4 floats, each half a sector: 8 sectors, 50%. Under the sector rule a warp needs runs of at least 8 floats; real hardware also prefers fewer distinct 128-byte lines per request (fewer L1 tag lookups), which is why 32-wide blocks are the default.
